  • lead to deterioration. Low-moisture foods have longer shelf life because microorganisms
  • cannot grow without sufficient water availability.

questions.question: What are the defects observed on fish spoilage? / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• What are the defects observed on fish spoilage? [U] / [CO5]
  • Fish spoils rapidly due to its high moisture, neutral pH, and abundant nutrients. Common spoilage
  • defects include surface slime caused by bacterial growth, softening and breakdown of muscle
  • tissues, and unpleasant odors such as fishy, sour, or ammonia-like smells. Visual changes include
  • dull eyes, pale gills, and discoloration of the skin or muscle. Advanced spoilage may cause belly
  • bursting due to gas production from bacteria like Shewanella. Texture deterioration and loss of
  • freshness are key indicators of spoilage.

questions.question: What are mycotoxins, and how are they related to mold spoilage? [U] [2]
questions.solution_html:
• Mycotoxins are toxic compounds produced by certain molds found in food and feed, posing health
  • risks to humans and animals. These toxins can contaminate crops both pre- and post-harvest, leading to
  • exposure through consumption of contaminated products. Mycotoxins exert their toxic effects through
  • complex biochemical interactions within the body. These compounds can disrupt cellular processes by
  • interfering with DNA replication and protein synthesis, leading to cellular damage and death. For
  • example, aflatoxins form reactive intermediates that bind to DNA, resulting in mutations and an
  • increased risk of cancer, particularly liver cancer. This interference with genetic material is a hallmark
  • of many mycotoxins and underscores their potential to cause long-term health issues.

questions.question: What is the role of p H in food spoilage. How does it affect microbial growth, enzymatic activity, and overall food safety? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is the role of pH in food spoilage. How does it affect microbial growth enzymatic
  • activity, and overall food safety? [U] / [CO3]
  • pH is a crucial intrinsic factor influencing food spoilage. Low pH (acidic foods) inhibits
  • many spoilage bacteria and pathogens, allowing mainly yeasts and molds to grow. High pH
  • foods, such as meat and fish, support rapid bacterial growth. pH also affects enzyme activity
  • many enzymes function optimally around neutral pH, causing nutrient breakdown and
  • chemical deterioration. Microbial toxins and spoilage metabolites vary with pH. By
  • controlling pH through fermentation or acidification, food safety is enhanced and shelf life is
  • prolonged.

questions.question: How does enzymatic spoilage differ from microbial spoilage? [An] [4]
questions.solution_html:
• Enzymatic spoilage is caused by the natural enzymes present within the food itself. These enzymes are
  • proteins that catalyze biochemical reactions and can cause changes in the food's texture, flavor, and
  • nutritional value over time. WhereasMicrobial spoilage is caused by microorganisms such as bacteria,
  • molds, and yeasts that grow and multiply on the food. These microorganisms thrive on the nutrients in
  • the food, breaking them down and often producing metabolic byproducts that cause spoilage.

questions.question: Comment on gas and alkali production in milk during spoilage. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Comment on gas and alkali production in milk during spoilage. [A] / [CO5]
  • Milk spoilage involves many microorganisms that break down milk components. Gas production
  • occurs mainly due to coliforms and Clostridium species, leading to frothiness, off-odors, and
  • bloating of containers. Alkali production occurs due to proteolytic bacteria such as
  • Pseudomonas, which degrade proteins into ammonia and amines. This increases the pH of milk,
  • producing bitter flavors and causing curdling. Both gas and alkali formation are advanced stages
  • of spoilage indicating microbial contamination and loss of milk quality.

questions.question: What is water activity (aw), and how is it measured? [U] [2]
questions.solution_html:
• Water activity (aw) is a measure of the available water in a substance that is free to interact with other
  • components (such as solutes, microbes, or enzymes) and participate in chemical and biological
  • reactions. In simple terms, water activity indicates how much of the water in a food, material, or
  • substance is not bound to other molecules (like salts, sugars, or proteins) and is available for microbial
  • growth, chemical reactions, and enzymatic activity.For example, lower water activity (such as in dried
  • foods) helps inhibit the growth of many microorganisms (including bacteria, mold, and yeast) and
  • slows down spoilage and degradation processes.
  • Water Activity Scale:
  • • Water activity is measured on a scale from 0 to 1, where:
  • o 0 means no available water (completely dry),
  • o 1.0 means pure water (with 100% of the water available

questions.question: Explain the role of bacteria, mold and yeast in food spoilage. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the role of bacteria, mold and yeast in food spoilage. [K] / [CO3]
  • Food spoilage is primarily caused by the activities of bacteria, molds, and yeasts, each
  • contributing differently based on food type and storage conditions.
  • Bacteria:
  • Bacteria are responsible for rapid spoilage in protein-rich and moist foods such as meat, fish,
  • milk, and vegetables. Psychrotrophic bacteria like Pseudomonas cause slime formation,
  • surface discoloration, and off-odors in refrigerated foods. Proteolytic bacteria break down
  • proteins into ammonia and sulfur compounds, causing putrefaction. Fermentative bacteria like
  • lactic acid bacteria cause souring in milk and vegetables. Anaerobic bacteria like Clostridium
  • cause gas production, bloating, and strong odors.
  • Molds:
  • Molds spoil foods with low moisture or acidic environments, including bread, fruits, and
  • stored grains. They produce visible mycelial growth and pigments that discolor food. Molds
  • cause spoilage through enzymatic breakdown of carbohydrates and organic acids. More
  • importantly, many molds produce mycotoxins such as aflatoxins and ochratoxins, which pose
  • serious health risks. Mold spoilage is common in improperly stored foods exposed to high
  • humidity.
  • Yeasts:
  • Yeasts spoil high-sugar and acidic foods such as juices, syrups, jams, and pickles. They cause
  • fermentation, gas production, and development of alcohols and esters that change taste and
  • smell. Yeasts such as Saccharomyces, Candida, and Zygosaccharomyces thrive in low pH
  • environments. Swelling of packaged food containers due to gas production is a common sign
  • of yeast spoilage.
  • Together, these microorganisms degrade food quality, reduce shelf life, and pose potential
  • health hazards.

questions.question: Describe what extrinsic factors are in the context of food spoilage. Discuss how these factors
questions.solution_html:
• differ from intrinsic factors.
  • In the context of food spoilage, extrinsic factors and intrinsic factors are two categories of
  • environmental conditions that influence the growth of microorganisms and the spoilage process of
  • food.
  • Extrinsic Factors- Temperature, Relative HumidityAtmosphere (Oxygen, Gases)Storage Conditions
  • and Time
  • Intrinsic Factors
  • Intrinsic factors, on the other hand, are properties inherent to the food itself. These factors are related to
  • the composition and structure of the food, which can influence its susceptibility to microbial growth
  • and spoilage. The main intrinsic factors include:
  • pH (Acidity/Alkalinity),Water Activity (aw)Nutrient ContentAntimicrobial Constituents , Structure
  • and Composition and Preservatives.
  • Differences Between Extrinsic and Intrinsic Factors
  • • Origin: Extrinsic factors come from the environment surrounding the food (temperature,
  • humidity, packaging, etc.), whereas intrinsic factors are inherent to the food itself (pH, water
  • activity, nutrient content).
  • • Control: Extrinsic factors are often more easily controlled during food storage and handling
  • (e.g., refrigeration, proper packaging), while intrinsic factors are fixed properties of the food
  • that cannot be easily changed (e.g., the natural acidity of citrus fruits).
  • • Effect on Microbial Growth: Extrinsic factors primarily influence the rate of microbial growth,
  • whereas intrinsic factors can either directly support or inhibit the types of microorganisms that
  • can grow on the food. For example, a high-water-activity food stored at room temperature will
  • spoil faster than a low-water-activity food, even if both have similar nutrient content.

questions.question: Write a note on factors that influence the invasion of micro-organisms in meat. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Write a note on factors that influence the invasion of micro-organisms in meat. [An] / [CO4]
  • Microbial invasion in meat is affected by multiple intrinsic and extrinsic factors:
  • • Animal factors: The health, stress level, and hygiene of the animal before slaughter
  • affect initial contamination. Diseased or stressed animals carry higher microbial loads.
  • • Slaughterhouse and processing hygiene: Contamination can occur from unclean
  • equipment, surfaces, water, or handlers. Contact with hides, digestive contents, or soil
  • introduces spoilage organisms.
  • • Environmental factors: Temperature, humidity, and air quality greatly influence
  • microbial growth. Warm and humid environments accelerate spoilage.
  • • Intrinsic factors of meat: Meat has high moisture, neutral pH, and abundant nutrients
  • that support microbial growth. The water activity (aw) of meat is favourable for bacteria
  • and fungi.
  • • Handling and storage: Improper cooling, delayed refrigeration, cross-contamination,
  • and poor packaging increase microbial invasion. Vacuum or modified-atmosphere
  • packaging slows down spoilage but cannot prevent it completely.
  • • Time-temperature abuse: The rate of microbial multiplication increases rapidly if meat
  • is stored above recommended temperatures.
  • Overall, spoilage can be minimized through strict hygiene, rapid chilling, and proper storage
  • and packaging.

questions.question: Evaluate the impact of microbial contamination on the shelf life of eggs? / [CO5] [1x10=10]
questions.solution_html:
• Evaluate the impact of microbial contamination on the shelf life of eggs? [E]/ [CO5]
  • Eggs, though protected by a shell, are highly vulnerable to microbial contamination when the
  • shell integrity is compromised or hygiene is poor. Contaminating microorganisms such as
  • Pseudomonas, Proteus, Salmonella, molds, and yeasts cause various types of spoilage
  • including black rot, green rot, red rot, and fungal growth. These microorganisms degrade egg
  • albumen, causing it to become watery, discolored, and foul-smelling. The yolk may also
  • liquefy and mix with the albumen due to enzyme activity. Microbial contamination
  • significantly reduces the shelf life of eggs as physical, chemical, and sensory qualities
  • deteriorate quickly. Contaminated eggs also pose a serious health risk, especially from
  • Salmonella infections. Proper washing, sanitizing, cooling, and storage at low temperatures
  • are essential to maintain egg quality and prevent spoilage.
